paper_title: SPLATIFY: Reproduce, Discover, Innovate! From Papers and Ideas to Trainable 3DGS Code

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The rapid growth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) research demands significant effort to reimplement papers before building on them. We introduce SPLATIFY, a multi-agent framework that converts 3DGS papers into trainable gsplat-based implementations, where generic paper-to-code methods and frontier models fail. SPLATIFY achieves this through five innovations: (1) A context-free grammar for gsplat over a modular method template with extension points for losses, densification, rendering, and optimization, constraining synthesis so generated code satisfies gsplat's architectural invariants by construction. (2) Architectural elements for faithful reproduction: fork-aware citation recovery retrieving component-level code at function-level granularity, Graph-of-Thought synthesis in topological dependency order, RAG-guided in-context example selection from over 20 verified implementations, and visual feedback combining PSNR-guided regeneration, Gaussian-level structural checks, and VLM-driven patching. (3) Knowledge-driven compositional improvement that autonomously finds weaknesses and composes complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies to improve upon original results. (4) Interdisciplinary method discovery where agents retrieve physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature and compose them with rendering knowledge to produce methods for previously unaddressed scene types. (5) SPLATIFY-Bench, an evaluation framework across 30 diverse 3DGS papers. On papers without public code, SPLATIFY matches expert implementations while reducing development time from weeks to minutes, and through compositional discovery further improves PSNR by up to 2.4 dB. We additionally demonstrate novel methods for volumetric nebula rendering and other scientific domains, synthesized entirely by SPLATIFY.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: SPLATIFY: Reproduce, Discover, Innovate! From Papers and Ideas to Trainable 3DGS Code Seemandhar Jain Keshav Gupta Manmohan Chandraker University of California, San Diego {sejain, keg019, mkchandraker}@ucsd.edu Figure 1. SPLATIFY: Reproduce, Discover, Innovate. Given 3DGS paper, SPLATIFY produces trainable gsplat code in minutes existing approaches cannot (Level 1), autonomously composes complementary techniques for up to +2.4 dB PSNR improvement for existing literature (Level 2), and invents entirely new methods by retrieving physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature (Level 3).

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The rapid growth of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) research demands significant effort to reimplement papers before building on them. We introduce SPLATIFY, multi-agent framework that converts 3DGS papers into trainable gsplatbased implementations, where generic paper-to-code methods and frontier models fail. SPLATIFY achieves this through five innovations: (1) context-free grammar for gsplat over modular method template with extension points for losses, densification, rendering, and optimization, constraining synthesis so generated code satisfies gsplats architectural invariants by construction. (2) Architectural elements for faithful reproduction: fork-aware citation recovery retrieving component-level code at function-level granularity, Graph-of-Thought synthesis in topological dependency order, RAG-guided in-context example selection from over 20 verified implementations, and visual feedback combining PSNR-guided regeneration, Gaussian-level structural checks, and VLM-driven patching. (3) Knowledge-driven compositional improvement that autonomously finds weaknesses and composes complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies to improve upon original results. (4) Interdisciplinary method discovery where agents retrieve physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature and compose them with rendering knowledge to produce methods for previously unaddressed scene types. (5) SPLATIFY-BENCH, an evaluation framework across 30 diverse 3DGS papers. On papers without public code, SPLATIFY matches expert implementations while reducing development time from weeks to minutes, and through compositional discovery further improves PSNR by up to 2.4 dB. We additionally demonstrate novel methods for volumetric nebula rendering and other scientific domains, synthesized entirely by SPLATIFY. Code, data, and all implementations will be publicly released. 1. Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting has triggered fast-growing subfield of neural rendering, yet the community publishes knowledge far faster than it can absorb. Since Kerbl et al. [28] introduced 3DGS in 2023, follow-up papers have grown to over 1,500 in under three years [7, 18], with track1 ing repositories recording roughly three new arXiv submissions per day [30]. For researcher who wants to use recently published method, however, the path from paper to working code remains prohibitively slow. Existing infrastructure cannot keep pace with this growth. While over 40% of tracked 3DGS papers release no code [2], others publish isolated forks with incompatible assumptions about attribute layouts, density control, rendering conventions [30], and CUDA kernels. Building on recent method typically demands weeks of manual reimplementation and debugging. Generic pipelines like Paper2Code [46] and AutoP2C [33] produce code that do not compile against any rasterization backend, and frontier models generate Python that collapses at training time for lack of domain knowledge about Gaussian attribute coupling or adaptive density control. No existing paper-to-code system, in any domain, handles 3DGSs fork-dominated landscape, provides Gaussian-level structural verification, or moves beyond reproduction to compositional improvement. Even if reproduction were perfectly solved, the deeper bottleneck would persist: the knowledge across 2k+ papers is neither discoverable nor composable. There is no efficient way to determine whether combining depth distortion loss from 2DGS [23] with stochastic splitting from 3DGS-MCMC [29] and an opacity regularizer from AbsGS [61] would outperform any of them individually. With hundreds of published techniques, the number of valid compositions is enormous, and manual exploration covers negligible fraction. Entire application domains where Gaussians are natural geometric fit, from optically thin nebulae to fluorescence microscopy, remain untouched because the engineering barrier is too high. The field needs infrastructure for discovering, composing, and extending the knowledge its papers contain. We introduce SPLATIFY  (Fig. 1)  , multi-agent framework operating at three levels: faithful reproduction of 3DGS papers as trainable gsplat [60] plugins, compositional improvement that autonomously combines complementary techniques, and cross-domain method invention for unaddressed scene types. Its design rests on five contributions: 1. context-free grammar for gsplat plugins over modular template with nine extension points covering the full 3DGS modification space, ensuring generated code satisfies architectural invariants by construction (Sec. 3.2). 2. Faithful reproduction extending the multi-stage pipeline of [25] with fork-aware citation recovery at function-level granularity, Gaussian-specific smoke tests, and PSNR training-curve monitoring (Sec. 3.3). 3. Compositional improvement through autonomous diagnosis of weaknesses in reproduced methods and composition of complementary regularizers, losses, and densification strategies from the knowledge base, yielding up to +2.4 dB PSNR gain with no human guidance (Sec. 3.4). 4. Cross-domain method invention, where agents retrieve physical priors from outside the 3DGS literature and synthesize physics-informed modifications for unaddressed domains such as volumetric nebula rendering and thinfilm bubble iridescence (Sec. 3.4). 5. SPLATIFY-Bench, 30-paper benchmark stratified by code availability and technical complexity (Sec. 4.1). On papers without public code, SPLATIFY matches expert implementations within 0.5 dB PSNR and 0.02 SSIM while existing baselines fail to produce trainable code. Crossdomain invention produces working methods for scene types no prior paper has addressed, entirely without human guidance. SPLATIFY, SPLATIFY-BENCH, all implementations, and the code will be publicly released. 2. Related Work The 3DGS Reproducibility Problem. 3D Gaussian Splatting [28] represents scenes as anisotropic Gaussians rasterized through differentiable tile-based renderer. The field has grown to over thousand papers [7, 18] spanning anti-aliasing [62], geometry [23], densification [29], and compression [16, 31]. We target gsplat [60] integrated with Nerfstudio [50] as the compilation target. fundamental barrier is the fragmented implementation landscape: most papers fork the original INRIA codebase into one-off repositories that resist comparison or reuse, demanding deeper domain awareness than any existing system provides. Automated Research Reproduction. Paper2Code [46] and AutoP2C [33] use staged parsing but produce non-trainable outputs for vision methods; AutoReproduce [68] and RePro [69] improve fidelity through citation lineage extraction yet remain domain-agnostic. PaperBench [48] quantifies the gap: the strongest agent scores 21% against 41.4% for human researchers on ICML papers. Multi-agent frameworks including MetaGPT [22], ChatDev [44], AutoGen [54], and repository-level agents [53, 56] advance role-specialized collaboration but lack scientific rendering-specific reasoning. The closest prior work is NERFIFY [25], which introduces grammar-constrained generation, compositional citation recovery, and visual feedback for NeRF-to-Nerfstudio synthesis. However, NERFIFY is limited to NeRFs, and 3DGS methods alter tightly coupled components across fragmented repository forks, unlike NeRF systems that modify relatively isolated neural modules. NERFIFY cannot handle this forkdominated ecosystem and lacks Gaussian-level verification. SPLATIFY adds fork-aware recovery via parent-repository diffs and Gaussian structural checks with PSNR curve monitoring, and goes beyond reproduction: it composes techniques to surpass the reproduced result and retrieves physical priors from outside the field for unaddressed scene types. Structured Reasoning and Iterative Code Refinement. Constraining LLM outputs with formal structure improves code correctness, as shown by pushdown-automaton decod2 paper has addressed, such as volumetric astronomical phenomena or fluorescence microscopy. Given target domain and multi-view training set, the agent retrieves physical priors Wphys from literature outside 3DGS, identifies which splatting assumptions are violated, and synthesizes physics-informed modifications within gsplat: CD = A(cid:0)D, Wphys; K, G(cid:1). Success is measured by improvement over vanilla 3DGS, cross-view consistency, and physical plausibility. This moves beyond translating existing knowledge toward generating new knowledge by bridging disciplinary boundaries. 3.2. CFG-Constrained gsplat Method Template Unconstrained LLM generation can produce code that looks plausible but violates framework invariants in ways that surface only at training time: dead optimizer entries, missing density-control bookkeeping, losses wired into the wrong module. Our solution is to formalize gsplat-based Nerfstudio plugins as CFG = (Σ, V, S, ) and provide agents with concrete method template instantiating this grammar as runnable code. This makes synthesis constrained task where agents decide which extension points papers contributions map to and what code to place there, while the structural skeleton is fixed by construction. Template design. By analysis of over 40 3DGS papers spanning anti-aliasing [62], geometry [23], densification [29], depth supervision, and feature distillation, we identify nine extension points covering the full modification space (listed in the supplementary). The templates core class GSTemplateModel inherits tile-based gsplat rasterization, adaptive density control, SH schedules, camera optimization, and the standard optimizer set. Agents subclass it and override only relevant hooks: compute custom losses() for new regularizer, or populate modules() plus split gaussians() for new per-Gaussian attribute. The grammar. Terminals Σ are framework classes, nonterminals are abstract components, S=PLUGIN is the start symbol, and productions encode valid compositions. The grammar serves two roles: it is included in every agents system prompt as structural specification, and it defines the verification contracts used during GoT synthesis (Sec. 3.3), where the master agent checks after each generated file that the repository remains valid derivation of G. An abbreviated version is shown in Fig. 3 Stage 1; the full grammar is in the supplementary. 3.3. Proposed Multi-Stage Framework Fig. 2 provides simplified view of the overall SPLATIFY pipeline, while Fig. 3 shows the complete system architecture. We design multi-stage framework similar to [25], but with several extensions and 3DGS-specific components, which are described below. Figure 2. Simplified SPLATIFY pipeline. high-level view of reproduction, refinement, and interdisciplinary method discovery. Fig. 3 shows the detailed architecture. ing [14], grammar prompting [51], and CFG-based visual program synthesis [65]. Iterative refinement through execution feedback is equally standard: Graph of Thoughts [5] and Tree of Thoughts [59] organize reasoning as searchable structures, while Self-Debugging [8], Reflexion [47], and Self-Refine [35] enable models to critique and repair their own outputs. SPLATIFY combines both: gsplat CFG guarantees architectural validity, while PSNR training-curve analysis and VLM-guided patching provide closed-loop feedback to converge on expert-quality implementations. 3. Proposed Approach 3.1. Problem Statement We consider three objectives of increasing scope: faithful reproduction, compositional improvement, and interdisciplinary method discovery. Faithful Reproduction. Given 3DGS paper P, we synthesize an executable repository = (F, G), where = {f1, . . . , fn} is set of source files and = BUILDREPODAG(F ) encodes their import and dataflow dependencies. parsing pipeline extracts structured information E(P) = T, I, Q, (text, figures, equations, bibliography) and passes it to our multi-agent system : (cid:0)E(P); R(cid:1) (cid:55) C. The resource tuple = (K, W, ) comprises CFG-grounded gsplat knowledge base (Sec. 3.2), web resources for cited papers and fork-level diffs, and library of verified implementations serving as in-context examples. Reproduction succeeds when compiles against gsplat, trains to convergence, and achieves rendering quality within ϵ = 0.5 dB PSNR of reported metrics while correctly implementing every novel component in P. Compositional Improvement. Many 3DGS methods address single weakness while remaining vulnerable to others. Given faithful reproduction C0 and library of verified techniques Ktech = {t1, .., tk} K, the agent uses visual feedback to find weaknesses, queries for complementary remedies, and validates that C+ = COMPOSE(C0, Ktech) remains valid grammar derivation and improves quality on held-out views. The agent receives no human guidance; it must independently diagnose, retrieve, and verify. Interdisciplinary Method Discovery. Reproduction (left): parsing agent structures papers into CFG-grounded knowledge base; fork-aware dependency resolution recovers components via citation graphs and repository diffs; GoT synthesis generates code in topological order with PSNR-guided and VLM-driven refinement. Knowledge discovery and invention (right): the populated knowledge base enables compositional improvement, where agents compose techniques to surpass original results, and interdisciplinary method creation, where physical priors from outside 3DGS literature are retrieved to address novel scene types. 3.3.1. sections.title: CFG
sections.content: SPLATIFY centers on the knowledge base and library of verified implementations = {(Pi, Ci)}X i=1, seeded with 20 manually validated papers. The agent first converts to structured markdown via MinerU [40], stripping nontechnical sections while preserving equations, pseudocode, diagrams, and citation relationships. For each new target, retrieval agent identifies the relevant extension points and selects the most similar subset of by extension-point overlap and technique type, so paper proposing regularization loss retrieves other regularization implementations. Any paper SPLATIFY successfully implements is automatically added back to , progressively broadening coverage. 3.3.2. Stage 2: Fork-Aware Compositional Dependency

sections.title: Resolution
sections.content: 3DGS papers are deeply compositional: single method routinely assembles rendering, regularization, densification, and post-processing components from many prior works. Unlike NeRF methods, which ship as standalone packages, roughly 70% of 3DGS papers release code as forks of the INRIA repository [28]. system that retrieves only text-level references misses these code-level dependencies entirely. Fork-aware recovery. The agent builds dependency graph via iterative multi-hop retrieval, identifying borrowed components, recursively resolving transitive dependencies, and terminating when all interface contracts are satisfied. The key departure from prior work is at the extraction step: for each cited paper, the agent checks whether its repository forks known base (3DGS, Mip-Splatting, 2DGS, Scaffold-GS), computes structured diff against the parent, and maps each changed function to semantic label (e.g., loss/depth distortion), yielding exact function-level contributions rather than noisy text-level citations. When no repository exists, the agent falls back to PDF-level extraction. Transitive fork chains are resolved by chaining diffs to recover the full modification stack. Running example. Figure 3 Stage 1 shows Trick-GS [1], which assembles 8 techniques from 7 papers: volume masking from Self-Organizing Gaussians [37], significance pruning from LightGaussian [16], SH band masking from E2ERD [52], progressive training from EAGLES [19] and SpecGaussian [58], progressive scales from RAIN-GS [27], and accelerated rasterization from Taming 3DGS [36]. Several of these fork INRIA 3DGS. Our agent diffs each fork against its parent  (Fig. 3)  , tags changed functions with semantic labels, and chains results across transitive edges, expanding the graph to 12 papers. Such depth is common: GaussianPro [10] spans 8 dependencies, while Scaffold-GS [34] and PGSR [6] each span 7. 3.3.3. Stage 3: Grammar-Guided Repository Generation The master agent orchestrates Graph-of-Thought (GoT) code generation approach exploiting the constrained structure of our method template. Since every plugin subclasses GSTemplateModel and inherits the full splatfacto training loop, rasterization, density control, and optimizer wiring, synthesis reduces to identifying extension points to which papers contributions map and filling in only the relevant 4 hooks. The agent classifies contributions into one or more of the nine extension points defined by G, verifies the selected combination before writing code, then generates files in topological order with DAG construction, interface freezing, implementation, and smoke testing. Most repositories pass within two iterations. 3.3.4. Stage 4: Visual-Driven Feedback After the system produces trainable code, we perform smoke training for 3k iterations and dispatch rendered images to critique agent operating on four branches  (Fig. 3)  : metric branch computing local-window PSNR and SSIM error maps, geometry branch flagging floaters and ghosting via cross-view artifact consensus, semantics branch using VLM to produce structured diagnoses with candidate patches, and training-curve branch unique to SPLATIFY. The last branch exploits key difference from NeRF: because 3DGS trains in minutes, the agent can monitor the full PSNR trajectory. 3DGS has structurally distinct densification phase terminating around 15k iterations, after which errors in pruning or loss schedules manifest as failures invisible during short smoke runs. The agent flags two modes: late-stage collapse (PSNR drops sharply post-15k) and stalled plateau (PSNR improves by less than 0.1 dB over any 5k-iteration window after warm-up). In both cases the agent localizes the fault to specific extension point and issues targeted patch. The loop continues until no further feedback is produced, the iteration budget is exhausted, or the papers reported PSNR is matched. 3.4. Knowledge Discovery via Evolutionary Technique Composition Beyond faithful reproduction, SPLATIFY operates in two modes (Fig. 3, right): compositional discovery, which improves synthesized implementation by composing complementary techniques from the 3DGS literature, and crossdomain invention, which retrieves physical priors from outside the field to address scene types no prior paper has tackled. Technique search space. The gsplat extension points define structured configuration = (D, L, A, M, ): mutually exclusive densification strategies (ADC, AbsGrad, MCMC), composable loss terms = 2{ℓ1,...,ℓn} (depth, normal, flatness, distortion), anti-aliasing options A, appearance models M, and continuous training-schedule parameters . Losses compose additively; densification strategies are mutually exclusive as they govern the same split-and-prune logic. For cross-domain invention, is augmented with physics-informed losses retrieved from outside the 3DGS literature. Evolutionary search. Inspired by FunSearch [45], we maintain K=8 islands each managed by an explorer agent. Each round proceeds in three steps  (Fig. 3)  : (1) each explorer proposes variant by mutating one axis of or composing an additional loss or strategy from when diagnosed weakness suggests it; (2) the Stage 3 pipeline converts each proposal into runnable gsplat code, evaluated via multifidelity cascade (2k7k30k iterations, eliminating the bottom half at each stage) to reduce per-round compute; (3) agents are ranked by Pareto sorting over normalized 0.4PSNR+0.3(1LPIPS)+0.3SSIM on subset of training views. The loop terminates when no agent improves for three consecutive rounds or the round budget is exhausted. For discovery, the search space is restricted to techniques already in K; for invention, the agents additionally query Wphys to retrieve domain-specific priors and propose physics-informed losses not present in any existing 3DGS paper. We demonstrate both modes in Sec. 4.5.1: compositional discovery yields up to +2.4 dB PSNR over the reproduction-only baseline, and cross-domain invention produces new methods for volumetric nebula rendering and thin-film bubble iridescence. 4. Experiments We evaluate SPLATIFY on SPLATIFY-BENCH, new benchmark for 3DGS paper-to-code synthesis, and present results on reproduction quality (Sec. 4.3), novelty preservation (Sec. 4.4), knowledge discovery (Sec. 4.5), and ablations. 4.1. SPLATIFY-BENCH Existing paper-to-code benchmarks [46, 48] evaluate general ML code generation and lack criteria specific to 3DGS, where implementations must coordinate Python-level training logic with CUDA rasterization backend, manage heuristic adaptive density control, and navigate fragmented ecosystem of forked repositories. SPLATIFY-BENCH is the first benchmark targeting this domain, comprising 30 papers across three sets. Set 1: Never-Implemented Papers (10). Papers with no publicly available code, paired with expert reference implementations we commissioned. Since no implementation exists online, LLMs cannot have encountered corresponding code during pretraining, ensuring uncontaminated evaluation. [11, 15, 17, 24, 39, 41, 43, 49, 55, 57] Set 2: Papers with Public Code (10). Papers with released repositories spanning densification strategies, regularization losses, and appearance modeling, all portable to gsplat, allowing direct comparison against original author code.[9, 12, 13, 20, 21, 28, 32, 38, 42, 67] Set 3: Novelty Coverage Papers (10). Papers chosen for the number and clarity of their distinct technical contributions, each with multiple verifiable novelty items (loss formulations, architectural modules, training schedules, Gaussian attribute modifications), used exclusively for the novelty analysis in Sec. 4.4. Baselines, Metrics, and Experimental Setup Baselines. We compare against five systems: generic paper-to-code pipelines Paper2Code [46] and AutoP2C [33]; frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.2 ET, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and DeepSeek 3.2; and expert implementations by researchers with 3DGS experience (typically 12 weeks per paper). SPLATIFY uses the full pipeline with GPT-5.2 as the base LLM for agents. All baselines were evaluated under the same setup: identical paper PDF and supplementary, prompts, and compute budget. Metrics. We report PSNR (dB), SSIM, LPIPS (lower is better), and Gaussian count (#GS, millions) as memory proxy. SPLATIFY completes in 1030 minutes per paper. API cost analysis is in the supplementary. Datasets and protocol. Our primary benchmark is MipNeRF 360 [4] (five outdoor, four indoor unbounded scenes). We follow the evaluation conventions of [3]. Every 8th image is held out for testing. We report on all nine scenes including the often-omitted flowers and treehill, and restrict Tanks and Temples to train and truck. All methods train for 30k iterations on identical data and test viewpoints on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs (48 GB), averaged on multiple seeds. Per-scene breakdowns are in the supplementary. Figure 4. Comparison to Expert Implementations 4.3.2. Set 2: Papers with Public Code 4.3.1. Set 1: Never-Implemented Papers We first evaluate SPLATIFY on papers for which no public implementation exists. This setting provides the strongest test of paper-driven synthesis capability: since no code for these methods has been released, the LLMs powering both our agents and the baselines cannot have encountered corresponding implementations during pretraining, ruling out data contamination. Expert developers required one to two weeks per paper to produce reference implementations, while SPLATIFY generates comparable code in minutes. Quantitative and Qualitative Results. Table 1 shows results for representative Set 1 papers, each evaluated under its own reported protocol (most average across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes; some report per-scene). SPLATIFY achieves visual quality within 0.5 dB PSNR and 0.02 SSIM of expert implementations on average, with qualitative comparisons shown in Fig. 4. All baselines fail to produce trainable code  (Table 2)  : generic systems cannot recover Table 3 compares SPLATIFY against original author repositories under identical training conditions. SPLATIFY achieves comparable performance with average deviations under 0.3 dB PSNR, while translating each method into standardized gsplat plugin within the Nerfstudio ecosystem for fair cross-method comparison. Although LLMs may have encountered these codebases during pretraining, baselines still fail to produce trainable code even with this potential advantage. 4.4. Novelty Coverage Analysis system that compiles and trains but silently drops novel loss term has failed at the task even if aggregate metrics appear reasonable. We evaluate novelty preservation on 10 papers from Set 3 using four metrics following [25]: (fraction correctly implemented), (partial/incorrect), (missing), and hyperparameter fidelity = {n : θn ˆθn < 0.1θn}/N . We additionally compute weighted semantic score ((cid:80) wi, where wi [0, 1] reflects component importance and si wisi)/ (cid:80) 6 {0, 0.2, . . . , 1.0} rates completeness, recognizing functionally equivalent implementations while penalizing semantic errors. All scoring is performed by Claude Opus 4.6 as an LLM judge, provided with the source paper, generated codes, and structured rubric; human experts with 3DGS development experience independently scored all components blind to system identity, agreeing with the judge at κ=0.87 on the C/I/M label and Spearman ρ=0.92 on the semantic score, reading each implementation function-by-function against its paper and flagging the exact baseline deviations (e.g., Euler angles for quaternions, Sigmoid vs Tanh opacity) independent of PSNR; they also verified every component added in compositional discovery and cross-domain invention. SPLATIFY attains near perfect scores with semantic scores above 0.94 across all papers  (Table 4)  . 4.5. Knowledge Discovery: Beyond Reproduction We now evaluate SPLATIFYs ability to go beyond faithful reproduction in two ways: improving already-reproduced methods by composing complementary techniques from the knowledge base, and synthesizing entirely new methods for scene types that no published paper has addressed. 4.5.1. Improving Existing Methods For papers in Set 1 and Set 2, we run second pass in which the agents query the knowledge base for techniques that address deficiencies identified during visual feedback. The agents receive no instructions about which techniques to apply; they must independently diagnose weaknesses, retrieve remedies, and validate that the composition improves quality. For comparison, we also ran the same loop with the explorer agents replaced by uniform random sampling over S. Random sampling used 8 times as many tokens and reached only quarter of the PSNR gain. Table 5 report results. Compositional discovery yields an improvement of up to +2.4 dB PSNR over the reproductiononly baseline. The goal is not to invent new primitives but to identify combinations of existing techniques that have not yet been explored; since the number of valid compositions grows quickly with published innovations, manual exploration of this space is infeasible. 4.5.2. Cross-Domain Method Creation All prior paper-to-code systems are limited to reproducing existing literature. We evaluate qualitatively different capability: given scene type that no published 3DGS paper has addressed, SPLATIFY retrieves physical priors from outside the 3DGS community and composes them with rendering knowledge to synthesize working method from scratch. We test on three domains where Gaussian primitives are natural geometric fit, but standard 3DGS fails due to mismatched physical assumptions. Both scenarios are human-verified at the code level. Figure 5 reports results. Figure 5. Cross-domain comparison. Ground truth, 3DGS, and agent-generated method for Nebula and Bubble. NebulaGS resolves opaque shell artifacts; BubbleGS captures iridescent color variation. Additional scenes in the supplementary. Tiαici where Ti = (cid:81) Scenario 1: Volumetric Nebula Rendering (NebulaGS). We evaluate on multi-view imagery of planetary nebula (157 training, 23 test views). Nebulae are optically thin emission media whose intensity is purely additive integral I(ν) = (cid:82) 0 jν(s) ds, with no absorption or occlusion. This directly conflicts with standard alpha compositing = (cid:80) j<i(1 αj), which drives opacities toward {0, 1} and produces opaque shell artifacts. Nebular emission also follows Kolmogorov turbulence with energy spectrum E(k) k5/3, placing significant detail at high spatial frequencies that pixel-space losses under-weight. The agents autonomously retrieved this radiative transfer and turbulence theory and identified six modifications: (i) an opacity ceiling loss (α < 0.95) suppressing opaque shells; (ii) per-Gaussian emission parameter decoupling brightness from opacity; (iii) spectral frequency loss via 2D FFT log-amplitude matching; (iv) scale isotropy penalty encouraging spherical Gaussians; (v) multi-scale L1 supervision to capture the Kolmogorov cascade; and (vi) SH degree set to 0. All modifications are training-time losses requiring no rasterizer changes. NebulaGS achieves 32.52 dB PSNR and 0.914 SSIM versus 31.19 dB and 0.862 for vanilla 3DGS (+1.33 dB, +0.052 SSIM), with per-view standard deviation dropping from 6.29 to 2.62 and rendering speed unaffected. Scenario 2: Iridescent Thin-Film Rendering (BubbleGS). Soap bubbles and oil slicks are dominated by thin-film interference. For film of thickness and refractive index nf 1.33, the optical path difference is δ = 2nf cos θt where θt follows Snells law nair sin θi = nf sin θt. (i) perGaussian film thickness parameter acting as soft segmentation; (ii) thin-film chrominance loss penalizing cosine distance between ˆcphys and rendered chrominance ˆcrender = c/c2; (iii) an opacity ceiling at α=0.45 for film Gaussians; (iv) shell flatness loss encouraging disk-like Gaussians; (v) total variation on the thickness map enforcing smooth drainage gradients; and (vi) L1 sparsity on thickness. All losses are gated on the learned thickness and require no rasterizer changes. BubbleGS achieves 27.81 dB PSNR and 0.869 SSIM versus 26.97 dB and 0.858 for vanilla 3DGS, with LPIPS improving from 0.264 to 0.244 and per-view standard deviation dropping from 8.23 to 4.85. Rendering speed decreases from 99.1 to 69.1 FPS due to the second thickness rasterization pass, though both remain well above real-time. Both scenarios are human-verified at the code level. The supplementary video shows SPLATIFY running end to end on live paper, from PDF to trainable gsplat plugin, followed by compositional discovery run. 4.6. Ablation Study Table 6 shows component ablations averaged over 10 Set 1 papers. CFG constraints have the largest impact on trainability (70% without, vs. 100% with), as agents misplace densification logic or wire optimizers incorrectly. Fork-aware recovery is equally critical: without it, 30% of novelties go unimplemented. Smoke tests account for the largest single trainability drop (50%), with Gaussian structural checks responsible for roughly half. PSNR curve monitoring catches late-stage failures invisible during short runs. One-shot generation without GoT collapses to score 0.49 despite high novelty fidelity, as agents produce monolithic files breaking dependency ordering. 5. Conclusion We presented SPLATIFY, multi-agent framework that converts 3DGS papers into trainable gsplat implementations through grammar-constrained synthesis, fork-aware citation recovery, and closed-loop visual feedback. On SPLATIFYBENCH, the framework matches expert implementations within 0.5 dB PSNR while all baselines fail to produce trainable code, reducing development time from weeks to minutes. Compositional discovery yields up to +2.4 dB PSNR gain, and cross-domain invention produces working methods for scene types no prior paper has addressed, entirely without human guidance. Generalizations, limitations, and reproducibility. The architectural elements of SPLATIFY are not specific to Gaussian Splatting; adapting to new domain such as 3D reconstruction pipelines or robotics simulation stacks requires defining CFG over that frameworks extension points and curating seed set of verified paper-code pairs. Code, data, and all generated implementations will be publicly released.
